verdict.summary: Registering a General app for your own account is quick and needs no review. Publishing for other users needs a Zoom security and functional review, and the broad default scope set (about 28 scopes) makes that review more likely to delay or trim scopes. Keeping the app private, or staying on Composio's managed app, avoids review entirely.
verdict.hands_on_effort: Gate 1: under 1 hour (estimate). Gate 3 (public listing): several days of documentation and listing prep (estimate), plus review wait.
verdict.time_to_first_connection: About 15-30 minutes once the Zoom for developers role is confirmed (estimate).
verdict.approval_wait: No official review completion SLA. Zoom states a 72-hour first response (typically about 36 hours). Community reports run from days to several weeks.

gates.name: Development credentials (unpublished General app, your own account)
gates.unlocks: Create the General app, get development client ID and secret, and connect your own Zoom account through your own OAuth app.
limits: Access tokens last 1 hour; refresh tokens expire after 90 days, then users must re-authorize.
Each refresh returns a new refresh token; always use the latest one.
No install cap or API rate limit for unpublished General apps was found.
gates.time_to_reach: Minutes, once the Developer role is available

gates.name: Private or beta app (invited/test users)
gates.unlocks: Private apps are for internal use. Beta apps let external testers authorize through an authorization URL before public release.
limits: Beta apps are not published to the Marketplace and need Zoom approval.
External beta testing is limited in number of users and time. No specific cap was found in the sources read.
gates.time_to_reach: Private: immediate after Gate 1. Beta: depends on Zoom approval (no published timeline).

gates.name: Public or unlisted Marketplace app (anyone can install)
gates.unlocks: Anyone can install the app from the Zoom App Marketplace (public) or via a direct link (unlisted).
limits: Public and unlisted apps go through Zoom's functional and security review.
Each requested scope needs a justification and test steps, or Zoom denies it.
Metadata and policy URLs must be on domains you own.
Scope changes after publishing need a new review (72-hour SLA), and existing users keep old authorization for 90 days.
Unpublishing returns the app to draft and requires full re-review to republish.
gates.time_to_reach: Submission prep plus review. First response within 72 hours (typically about 36). Full completion time not published.

steps.title: Confirm your account can create developer apps
steps.detail: You must be the Zoom account owner, an account admin, or hold the 'Zoom for developers' role. Without that role the Developer link does not appear in the Marketplace. If you lack it, ask an admin to go to User Management > Roles, open the role's advanced features, and tick View and Edit for 'Zoom for developers'.

values.label: Required role
values.value: Account owner, account admin, or 'Zoom for developers' role

gotchas: Free accounts can build and publish, but must either upgrade to Free with Credit Card or submit Zoom's developer-information form (U.S. sanctions compliance).

steps.title: Complete the free-account compliance step if it applies
steps.detail: If you are on a free account, either upgrade with a credit card or submit Zoom's developer-information form before you publish. This is a one-time account requirement, not an app review.

steps.title: Create the General app
steps.detail: Sign in to the Zoom App Marketplace at marketplace.zoom.us, open Develop, choose Build an app, select General app, then click Create. General app is the User OAuth type. Do not use Server-to-Server OAuth for this, because that type manages your own account without user consent.

values.label: Menu path
values.value: Develop > Build an app > General app > Create

steps.title: Choose the app audience
steps.detail: Decide whether the app is account-level (added across an account by admins) or user-managed (each user adds it). If the audience is 'Users within my Zoom account', the app is internal and skips the standard Marketplace review. External users require review.

steps.title: Set the OAuth redirect URL and allow list
steps.detail: In the app's OAuth settings, enter the redirect URL and add it to the OAuth allow list. Both are required. Use the exact callback URL from your Composio auth config. Redirects must be HTTPS. Custom URL schemes are only for Meeting SDK apps, and loopback (127.0.0.1) only works for PKCE or native clients.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: A redirect that does not exactly match the registered URL will fail the authorization.

steps.title: Copy credentials and connect your own account
steps.detail: Copy the development client ID and client secret that Zoom generates for the app. Enter them in your Composio auth config for Zoom (Composio custom app mode), then authorize with your own Zoom account. Confirm that a token refresh works, because refresh tokens rotate.

values.label: Credentials
values.value: Development client ID and client secret (use production credentials only at publish time)

gotchas: Access tokens last 1 hour. Refresh tokens expire after 90 days, so plan for re-authorization.
Always store the newest refresh token returned by each refresh call.

steps.title: Decide whether you need PKCE (public client)
steps.detail: Only turn this on if your client cannot keep a secret. Toggle Use Public Client OAuth to on in App Credentials to get a client ID with no secret. Public clients must use the S256 challenge method. Public apps may need a production explanation of why they require a public client ID.
gotchas: Loopback redirects are allowed only for PKCE-enabled or native clients.

steps.title: Trim the scope list
steps.detail: Start from the scopes Composio requests and remove any your agent does not use. Mark each remaining scope as required or optional. Every scope you keep becomes a request to Zoom's Security Review team, and unused scopes can be denied.
gotchas: Zoom's reviewers may ask you to remove unused or inappropriate scopes, even after you submit.

steps.title: Test with private or beta users
steps.detail: Keep the app private while you test with your own account or internal users. Private apps skip review. If you need external testers before public release, use a beta app; it is not published and needs Zoom approval before testers can use it. Expect limits on user count and time.
gotchas: The sources do not state a specific beta user cap or time limit. Confirm in the Zoom console before you rely on it.

steps.title: Prepare the review package
steps.detail: Draft a Scope Description for each scope that explains why the app needs it, plus step-by-step test instructions for each scope. Draft a test plan (document or demo video) and fill in the Technical Design section covering architecture, security controls, and how the app uses Zoom data. Draft Terms, Support, Privacy Policy, and Documentation pages.

values.label: Scope Description field
values.value: Explain how each requested scope is necessary for the app

gotchas: Without justifications and test steps, Zoom denies the scope and asks for it to be removed.
Policy and resource pages cannot be hosted on Google Drive or Dropbox. Use domains you own.

steps.title: Set up the deauthorization webhook and domain
steps.detail: Set the deauthorization endpoint on your listing. When a user removes the app, Zoom posts an app_deauthorized event, and you must delete that user's data. Zoom also runs a one-time check that the domain receiving callbacks is yours. Use the same domain for the OAuth redirect and webhook.

steps.title: Write the listing
steps.detail: Write a description of 150 characters or fewer. Upload 2 to 3 gallery images at 1200 x 780 px. Publish user docs covering adding, using, and removing the app. Provide a support URL with support hours and a first-response time for published apps.

steps.title: Submit with the production client ID
steps.detail: Switch to the production client ID and secret, then submit the app for review from the app's Marketplace page. The first submission for a new app uses the production client ID. Your production redirect must match the one in the authorization URL, because reviewers authorize with the production client ID. Complete the public-client explanation if you turned on PKCE.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: Update submissions use the development client ID, not production.

steps.title: Wait for Zoom's review
steps.detail: Zoom's stated first response is within 72 hours, typically about 36 hours. Full review has no published completion time; community reports range from days to several weeks, with the security review possibly adding up to about two weeks after functional review. Clear scopes and a clear test plan shorten review.

steps.title: Plan for post-publish changes
steps.detail: Adding scopes or changing data access to a published app requires functional and security review, with the 72-hour SLA. Existing users keep their old authorization for 90 days, then must re-authorize. Community reports say scope-adding updates do not skip the queue. Unpublishing returns the app to draft and requires full re-review.
gotchas: Scope changes after launch are the most likely cause of a second review.

scopes.effect: Transcript read and delete access to user data. Expect Zoom to ask why delete is needed; drop it if the agent does not delete transcripts.
Write access that changes user meetings and registrations. Each needs a justification and test steps.
Reads account profile and settings. Likely easy to justify only if the agent uses them; remove if unused.
Mark each scope required or optional. Optional scopes can let users decline without blocking sign-in.
No official source found on whether any scope is sensitive or restricted, or how that changes review depth. Confirm in the Scopes page before submission.

blockers.symptom: The 'Developer' link does not appear in the Zoom Marketplace.
blockers.cause: Your account lacks the account owner, admin, or 'Zoom for developers' role.
blockers.fix: Ask an account admin to enable View and Edit for 'Zoom for developers' under User Management > Roles, or ask the admin to create the app.

blockers.symptom: Zoom denies scopes and asks you to remove them during review.
blockers.cause: Missing per-scope justifications or test steps, or scopes that are unused or redundant.
blockers.fix: Write a Scope Description and test steps for each scope, and remove any scope the app does not call.

blockers.symptom: Submission rejected because policy or support documents are on Google Drive or Dropbox.
blockers.cause: Metadata URLs must be on domains you own.
blockers.fix: Host Terms, Privacy Policy, Support, and Documentation on your own domain.

blockers.symptom: Authorization fails with a redirect error when you use a custom scheme or 127.0.0.1 redirect.
blockers.cause: Custom URL schemes are for Meeting SDK apps only, and loopback works only for PKCE or native clients.
blockers.fix: Use an HTTPS redirect that matches the Composio callback URL in your allow list.

blockers.symptom: Reviewers' authorization fails or the redirect does not match during review.
blockers.cause: Reviewers authorize with the production client ID, and the redirect in the authorization URL must match the production redirect.
blockers.fix: Register the same Composio callback URL under the production credentials before submitting.

blockers.symptom: Scope added after launch sends the app back into review.
blockers.cause: Scope changes to a published app go through functional and security review.
blockers.fix: Finalize the scope list before the first submission. Plan for up to 72 hours for the scope review, and a 90-day window before old authorizations expire.

composio.note: Start on Composio's managed Zoom OAuth unless you need your own client ID and secret, your own branding or redirect URI, or distribution beyond your own account. The managed flow uses Composio's own callback and about 28 default user-level scopes. If you register your own General app, you must review and trim those scopes, paste the Composio callback URL shown in your auth config into Zoom, and go through Zoom review before any outside user can connect.

evidence.claim: Composio reports managed OAuth for Zoom, with OAUTH2 and zoom.us authorize and token endpoints.
evidence.quote: "managed_oauth_available": true, "authorization_url": "https://zoom.us/oauth/authorize"

evidence.claim: Composio's default Zoom auth config requests about 28 granular user-level scopes and redirects to Composio's own backend.
evidence.quote: "default_redirect_uri": "https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add"

evidence.claim: Zoom's OAuth app is created in the Zoom App Marketplace and can be account-level (admins) or user-managed (individual users).
evidence.quote: This app type can be either added and managed across an account by account admins (account-level app) or by users individually (user-managed app).

evidence.claim: You must be the account owner, an account admin, or hold the 'Zoom for developers' role; otherwise the Developer link does not appear.
evidence.quote: You are either the Zoom account owner, account admin, or have been assigned the Zoom for developers role.

evidence.claim: An admin grants the developer role by ticking View and Edit for 'Zoom for developers' in the role's advanced features under User Management > Roles.
evidence.quote: Select the View and Edit checkboxes for Zoom for developers.

evidence.claim: Creation steps: Develop > Build an app, select General app, then click Create. General app is the OAuth app type.
evidence.quote: On the app creation screen, select General app and click Create.

evidence.claim: The build flow generates a client ID and secret; development credentials are for testing and production credentials are for publishing.
evidence.quote: Use production credentials once you are ready to publish your app on the Marketplace.

evidence.claim: An OAuth redirect URL and an OAuth allow list are both required.
evidence.quote: OAuth allow lists (required): Add any unique URLs that Zoom should allow as valid redirects for your OAuth flows.

evidence.claim: Custom URL schemes for redirects are supported only for Meeting SDK apps, so General OAuth apps need HTTPS redirects.
evidence.quote: The build flow supports custom URL schemes only for Zoom Meeting SDK apps.

evidence.claim: Loopback redirects work only for PKCE-enabled or native clients; simple non-PKCE apps must use HTTPS.
evidence.quote: Do not use loopback for simple OAuth apps that are not PKCE-enabled and native apps.

evidence.claim: Turning on Use Public Client OAuth in App Credentials gives a public client ID with no secret; public clients must use S256.
evidence.quote: Toggle Use Public Client OAuth to on.

evidence.claim: Public-client apps may need to explain in their production submission why they need a public client ID and which flow they use.
evidence.quote: If you make your app public, you may need to add an explanation why your application requires a public client ID in production.

evidence.claim: Access tokens last one hour; refresh tokens expire after 90 days, then users must re-authorize.
evidence.quote: Refresh tokens expire after 90 days. You should always use the latest refresh token for the next refresh request.

evidence.claim: Each refresh response returns a new refresh token, and the latest must be used for the next refresh.
evidence.quote: You should always use the latest refresh token for the next refresh request.

evidence.claim: On removal of a production app, Zoom posts app_deauthorized to the listing endpoint; the app must delete that user's data. Tokens can be revoked at zoom.us/oauth/revoke.
evidence.quote: After receiving a deauthorization webhook event, apps must delete all associated user data.

evidence.claim: New apps use granular scopes, and each scope can be marked required or optional.
evidence.quote: New apps can also set which scopes are required and which are optional.

evidence.claim: Adding a scope is a request to Zoom's Security Review team, which may reject scopes it considers unnecessary.
evidence.quote: When you add a scope, you are actually submitting a request to the Zoom Security Review team

evidence.claim: The Security Review checks for minimum scopes and may ask developers to drop unused or inappropriate scopes.
evidence.quote: Developers may be asked to remove unused or inappropriate scopes.

evidence.claim: Each scope needs a justification and step-by-step test instructions; without them Zoom denies the scope and asks for removal.
evidence.quote: Without them, we deny the rest and request the removal of the scope.

evidence.claim: A scope change to a published app needs functional and security review under the standard 72-hour SLA.
evidence.quote: Changes to scope, features, or data access need to go through both a functional review and a security review and fall within our standard 72 hour response SLA.

evidence.claim: Users who authorized before a scope-changing update keep their authorization for 90 days, then must re-authorize.
evidence.quote: Existing users can continue using their current authorization for 90 days.

evidence.claim: Only public and unlisted apps go through Zoom's review; private and beta apps are stated to skip it.
evidence.quote: Private and beta apps do not require review.

evidence.claim: Every submission must include a completed Technical Design section covering architecture, security controls, and data use from OAuth scopes.
evidence.quote: all developers must complete the Technical Design section of the build flow.

evidence.claim: A test plan (document or demo video) is required for each submission, including resubmissions.
evidence.quote: A test plan is required for each submission, including re-submissions.

evidence.claim: The production client ID is used for the first submission of a new app; the development client ID is used for update submissions.
evidence.quote: Production client ID: Use this for the initial review submission for new apps.

evidence.claim: Terms, Support, Privacy Policy and Documentation URLs must be on domains the company owns; Google Drive and Dropbox hosting is not allowed.
evidence.quote: Hosting these documents on third-party platforms like Google Drive or Dropbox is not permitted.

evidence.claim: Zoom runs a one-time domain check that the domain receiving callbacks is owned by the developer.
evidence.quote: We perform a one-time verification to make sure that the domain where you receive Zoom callbacks is owned by you.

evidence.claim: Listing needs user docs, 2 to 3 gallery images at 1200 x 780 px, a description of 150 characters or fewer, and a support URL with hours and first-response SLA.
evidence.quote: Include 2 to 3 images that show what a user can expect with the integration.

evidence.claim: Free-account developers can build and publish but must upgrade with a credit card or submit Zoom's developer-information form.
evidence.quote: Zoom allows free accounts to develop and publish apps.

evidence.claim: Apps with the 'Users within my Zoom account' audience are internal and skip the standard Marketplace review.
evidence.quote: These apps are intended for internal use and don't require the standard Marketplace review.

evidence.claim: Beta apps are not published, distribute through an authorization URL, and need Zoom approval; external testing is limited in users and time.
evidence.quote: Beta apps are intended for external testing before public release; they are not published to the Zoom App Marketplace.

evidence.claim: Zoom publishes no completion time for review; clear scopes and a clear test plan shorten it.
evidence.quote: Testing time is typically the shortest for apps that have properly defined scopes, a clear test plan, and clear descriptive content for listing information.

evidence.claim: Zoom's developer blog states a 72-hour first-response SLA, typically responding within 36 hours.
evidence.quote: We have a 72 hour first response SLA, and typically respond within 36 hours of your submission.

evidence.claim: A developer-forum post reports the security review can take up to about two weeks after functional review. Anecdote, not an SLA.
evidence.quote: After you complete the functional review, the security review can take up to 2 weeks

evidence.claim: A community guide notes that an update adding new OAuth scopes goes through a fresh security review.
evidence.quote: if you release an update that requires new OAuth scopes, you don't get to bypass the line

evidence.claim: Unpublishing returns the app to draft and requires full re-review before republishing; default removal is 30 days.
evidence.quote: By default, the app is scheduled for removal or unpublishing in 30 days.

evidence.claim: No install cap or API rate limit for unpublished General apps was found.
evidence.quote: There are no rate limits per loopback.

evidence.claim: Server-to-server OAuth is a separate app type for managing your own account without user consent; use General app when users authorize access to their data.
evidence.quote: To build an app that provides server-to-server interaction with Zoom APIs to manage your account, create a server-to-server OAuth app.

evidence.claim: Developer-forum threads report approval waits of several weeks, beyond the stated SLA. Anecdotes.
evidence.quote: App Approval Process takes more than 7+ Weeks

evidence.claim: A practitioner account from October 2026 says reviewers authorize with the production client ID, and the redirect must match the production redirect.
evidence.quote: Reviewers authorise with the Production client ID.

evidence.claim: The Scope Description field requires the developer to explain why each requested scope is needed.
evidence.quote: In the Scope Description field, explain how the requested scope is necessary for your app.

open_questions: Whether Composio's managed Zoom app is published in the Zoom Marketplace or runs as a private app was not verified. Its default redirect goes to Composio's backend, so your own app would not be used in that flow.

Conflict: one finding says private and beta apps skip review, while another says beta apps need Zoom approval before testers can use them. Confirm in the Zoom console which applies to your audience before relying on beta.
No official sensitive or restricted classification was found for the scopes, and no source explains how it changes review depth.
No official install cap, beta user cap, or time limit was found for unpublished General apps.
No official review completion SLA was found. Only the 72-hour first-response SLA and community timelines of days to weeks were located.
Whether a paid plan is required for an external listing was not confirmed. Free accounts can publish after the compliance step.
Business verification or organization-entity requirements for a listing were not found in the sources read.
Linked pages not fetched: check-review-status, publish, and app-listing pages.
Legacy OAuth, Chatbot, and Meeting SDK app types were consolidated into General app. Setups created before this may differ.
